title: Docker layer caching
content: Docker builds each Dockerfile instruction into its own image layer, and it reuses a cached layer whenever the instruction and its inputs haven't changed since the last build. Because layers are cached in order, a single change early in the file - like editing application source before installing dependencies - invalidates every layer that follows it, even the expensive npm install or apt-get step below. That's why the common trick is to copy only the dependency manifest (package.json, requirements.txt) and install first, then copy the rest of the source afterward: dependency layers stay cached across most rebuilds. BuildKit's cache mounts extend this further by persisting a directory like ~/.cache/pip across builds even when the layer itself is invalidated.

title: HTTP caching headers
content: Cache-Control replaced the older Expires and Pragma headers as the primary way an HTTP response tells a client (or an intermediate proxy) how long it may reuse a response without asking the origin again; max-age=3600 means the resource is fresh for one hour from the response's Date. ETag and Last-Modified support a second, complementary mechanism called revalidation: once a cached copy goes stale, the client can send If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since, and the server replies with a bodiless 304 Not Modified if nothing actually changed, saving the transfer even though a round trip still happens. Setting Cache-Control: no-store forbids caching entirely, which is different from no-cache, which still permits storage but forces revalidation before every reuse. private vs public controls whether a shared proxy or CDN is allowed to cache the response at all, which matters for anything containing per-user data.

title: SQLite WAL mode
content: In SQLite's default rollback-journal mode, writers hold an exclusive lock that blocks all readers for the duration of a transaction; WAL (write-ahead logging) mode instead appends new pages to a separate -wal file and lets readers keep working against the last-checkpointed state while a single writer appends concurrently, so readers and the writer no longer block each other. A checkpoint periodically copies the WAL's contents back into the main database file and truncates it; if a process dies mid-checkpoint the database recovers cleanly on next open because the WAL is replayed. WAL mode requires the database to live on a filesystem that supports shared memory (mmap), which rules out most network filesystems, and it's a per-database-file setting enabled once with PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL.

title: DNS resolution order
content: When an application looks up a hostname, the OS resolver typically checks several sources before ever sending a packet over the network: first the local hosts file (e.g. /etc/hosts on Linux/macOS), then whatever is configured in nsswitch.conf, which usually points at a local stub resolver or systemd-resolved, and only after those are exhausted does a recursive query go out to the configured DNS server. The recursive resolver itself walks the hierarchy from a root server down to the TLD server down to the authoritative nameserver unless it already has a cached answer within the record's TTL. Because the hosts file is checked first, an entry there overrides whatever the actual DNS records say, which is a common source of confusing 'it works on my machine but not in prod' bugs.

title: JWT expiry handling
content: A JWT's exp claim is a Unix timestamp the server checks on every request; once the current time passes it, the token must be rejected regardless of its signature validity, so a compromised-but-expired token stops being useful without any revocation infrastructure. Because JWTs are stateless and can't be individually revoked before they expire, the common pattern is to keep access-token lifetimes short (minutes) and pair them with a separate, longer-lived refresh token that's stored server-side (or as an opaque, revocable value) and used to mint a new access token. Clock skew between the issuer and the verifier is a real failure mode, so most libraries apply a small leeway (30-60 seconds) when comparing exp and nbf against the local clock.

title: Kubernetes readiness probes
content: A readiness probe tells Kubernetes whether a pod is currently able to serve traffic; when it fails, the kubelet removes the pod's endpoint from the Service so no new requests are routed to it, but - unlike a failing liveness probe - the container is not restarted, since the pod may just be temporarily busy (draining a queue, warming a cache) rather than broken. This distinction matters most during rollouts: a Deployment won't consider a new pod available, and won't proceed to the next batch of the rolling update, until its readiness probe starts passing, which is what prevents traffic from hitting a pod that hasn't finished loading its config yet. Startup probes exist for the same reason but for slow-starting containers, disabling the other two probes' failure counting until the app reports it has finished booting.

title: Sourdough hydration
content: Hydration is just the ratio of water to flour by weight, so a dough at 75% hydration has 75g of water for every 100g of flour; most sourdough loaves fall somewhere between 65% (easier to shape, tighter crumb) and 85% (stickier, more open and irregular crumb, harder to handle without practice). Higher hydration doughs ferment a bit faster because more free water speeds enzyme activity, and gluten development is easier to achieve through folds rather than kneading. Bakers usually raise hydration gradually as they get comfortable with handling wetter dough rather than jumping straight to a wet formula, since a dough that's too slack to hold its shape during proofing will spread flat rather than rise.

title: Espresso grind size
content: Grind size is the main lever for controlling espresso extraction time: too coarse and water rushes through in under 20 seconds, pulling a thin, sour, under-extracted shot; too fine and the puck resists flow so much that the shot chokes, taking 40+ seconds and turning bitter and over-extracted. The target is usually 25-30 seconds for roughly 2 ounces of output from a double shot, and grinders need to be adjusted in tiny increments because espresso's short contact time makes it far more sensitive to particle size than drip or pour-over. Because grind size interacts with dose, tamp pressure, and bean freshness, changing beans or letting them rest longer usually means re-dialing the grind rather than reusing yesterday's setting.

title: Kafka consumer rebalancing
content:
Kafka distributes the partitions of a topic across the consumers in a consumer group so that each partition is read by exactly one consumer within that group at a time. This assignment isn't fixed forever - it's recomputed by a process called a rebalance whenever group membership changes, and the coordinator broker for that group is responsible for driving it.

A rebalance is triggered by a handful of events: a consumer joins or leaves the group (including a graceful shutdown), a consumer is judged dead because it stopped sending heartbeats within session.timeout.ms, a consumer takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms to call poll() again (which the broker treats identically to a crash even though the process is alive), or the topic's partition count changes. When any of these happens, the group coordinator revokes every partition assignment in the group and redistributes them among the surviving members according to the group's configured assignment strategy.

The classic 'stop-the-world' eager rebalance protocol requires every consumer to give up all of its partitions before the new assignment is computed, which means the entire group stops consuming for the duration of the rebalance - potentially seconds on a large group. Cooperative (incremental) rebalancing, the default strategy in modern clients, instead only reassigns the specific partitions that actually need to move, letting consumers keep processing their unaffected partitions throughout.

The practical consequence for anyone running a consumer is that unprocessed offsets and slow message processing are the two biggest causes of unwanted rebalances: if a single poll() loop iteration can take longer than max.poll.interval.ms (for example while making a slow downstream call), Kafka will conclude the consumer died and kick it out of the group, triggering a rebalance and duplicate processing on whichever consumer picks up the abandoned partition next.

title: Postgres index types
content:
Postgres ships with several index access methods, and choosing the wrong one for a query pattern is one of the most common sources of an unexpectedly slow plan. B-tree, the default and by far the most common, supports equality and range comparisons (<, <=, =, >=, >) and is the only index type that can also enforce a UNIQUE constraint; it's the right default unless you have a specific reason to reach for something else.

GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes are built for columns containing multiple values per row - arrays, jsonb documents, and full-text search tsvector columns. Rather than storing one entry per row, GIN stores one entry per distinct component value pointing back to every row that contains it, which makes 'does this array contain X' or 'does this jsonb have this key' queries fast at the cost of slower writes and larger index size than a B-tree.

GiST (Generalized Search Tree) indexes are the go-to for geometric data and range types, and they're what PostGIS builds on for spatial queries; they support 'nearest neighbor' and overlap queries that a B-tree structurally cannot answer, because GiST supports lossy, overlapping regions in a way a strictly ordered tree does not. BRIN (Block Range Index) takes the opposite approach from GIN: instead of indexing every value, it stores only the min/max range of a column for each physical block of the table, which produces indexes that are tiny compared to a B-tree and works well specifically when a column correlates with physical insertion order - a timestamp column on an append-only events table is the textbook case.

Hash indexes support only equality lookups, never ranges, and for a long time were avoided because they weren't crash-safe or replicated in WAL; since Postgres 10 that's no longer true, but a B-tree on the same column is usually just as fast for equality and additionally supports range queries, so hash indexes see fairly narrow use today. The general decision process is: B-tree unless the data shape is specifically array/JSON/full-text (GIN), geometric/range (GiST), or a huge naturally-ordered append-only table where index size matters more than lookup precision (BRIN).

title: Python asyncio task cancellation
content:
Cancelling an asyncio task doesn't stop it immediately - calling task.cancel() merely schedules a CancelledError to be raised at the next point the task is suspended on an await, which means a task doing pure CPU-bound work between awaits keeps running until it reaches one. Because of this, a task can catch CancelledError just like any other exception, and if it swallows it without re-raising, the task simply continues running as though nothing happened, which silently breaks cancellation for whatever code requested it.

The safe pattern for cleanup is a try/finally around the awaited work, or an except asyncio.CancelledError: raise if any cleanup logic is needed before propagating - never a bare except Exception, because in versions before 3.8 CancelledError inherited from Exception, and even now a broad except silently absorbs it in the same way. Since Python 3.8, CancelledError inherits directly from BaseException specifically so that generic exception handlers don't accidentally catch it.

Cancellation gets meaningfully harder once a task is awaiting something that isn't itself cancellation-aware - a call into a synchronous C extension via a thread pool executor, for instance, can't be interrupted mid-call; the cancellation only takes effect once control returns to the event loop. asyncio.shield() exists for the opposite problem: wrapping an inner awaitable so that cancelling the outer task doesn't propagate cancellation into the shielded one, useful when a cleanup or commit operation must run to completion even if the caller gave up waiting for it.

asyncio.timeout() (3.11+) and the older asyncio.wait_for() are both built on cancellation under the hood - they cancel the wrapped coroutine when the deadline passes and then raise TimeoutError to the caller, so a timeout and a caller-initiated cancellation look identical from inside the coroutine being cancelled and need the same cleanup discipline.

title: TLS certificate chains
content:
A TLS certificate is signed by whichever authority issued it, and that issuer's own certificate is in turn typically signed by another, forming a chain that terminates at a root certificate - a self-signed certificate that's built into the operating system's or browser's trust store rather than being verified by anything further up. Verifying a chain means walking it from the leaf (the server's own certificate) up through zero or more intermediates until reaching a root the client already trusts, checking at each link that the signature was produced by the private key matching the next certificate up.

Root CAs deliberately don't sign server certificates directly; instead they sign intermediate CA certificates, and those intermediates sign the certificates actual servers present. This exists mainly for risk containment: a root's private key is kept offline in a vault and used only rarely, so if an intermediate is ever compromised it can be revoked without invalidating the root or forcing every trust store on earth to be updated.

A very common misconfiguration is a server that sends only its leaf certificate and omits the intermediate(s). Browsers often still work in this case because they cache intermediates they've seen before or can fetch them via the AIA (Authority Information Access) extension, but many non-browser clients - a bare curl invocation, a backend service's HTTP client, a mobile app on a device without that cached intermediate - will fail chain validation outright, which is why 'works in Chrome but fails from our server' is such a recognizable TLS support ticket.

Expiry is checked at every level of the chain, not just the leaf: if an intermediate certificate expires, every certificate it issued becomes untrusted the moment that expiry passes, even if the leaf certificate's own notAfter date is still far in the future. This is why a batch of certificates issued under the same intermediate can all break simultaneously on a date nobody was individually tracking.

title: Vector database tradeoffs
content:
A vector database's job is approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search over high-dimensional embeddings, and the central tradeoff across every implementation is recall versus latency: an exact brute-force scan guarantees the true nearest neighbors but costs O(n) per query, while an ANN index trades a small, tunable chance of missing the true nearest neighbor for query times that barely grow with the size of the collection.

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graphs are the dominant approach in most of today's popular options (pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate) because they offer strong recall at low latency, but they hold the entire graph in memory and rebuilding or bulk-inserting into one is comparatively expensive, which makes HNSW better suited to read-heavy, append-light workloads than to a collection that's rewritten constantly. IVF (inverted file index) approaches instead cluster vectors ahead of time and only search the clusters nearest the query vector, trading some recall for an index that's cheaper to build and update, which is part of why FAISS and some larger-scale systems favor IVF variants for huge collections that need periodic rebuilding.

The other axis, separate from the ANN algorithm itself, is whether the vector store is a dedicated system (Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate) or a vector index bolted onto an existing database (pgvector inside Postgres, or a vector column in a document store). A dedicated system is usually built from the ground up around embeddings - filtering, sharding, and horizontal scaling designed for hundreds of millions of vectors - while an embedded index avoids operating a second system and lets a query join a similarity search against relational filters in one place, at the cost of scaling only about as far as the host database does.

For a system under a few million vectors and moderate query volume, the honest answer is that the choice of ANN algorithm and even the choice of dedicated-vs-embedded rarely dominate; a brute-force scan is single-digit milliseconds at that scale, and the tradeoffs above only start to bite in the tens-of-millions-of-vectors range or under very high query throughput, at which point rebuild cost, memory footprint, and horizontal scalability become the deciding factors rather than raw recall.

title: CAP theorem
content:
The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can provide at most two of three guarantees simultaneously during a network partition: consistency (every read sees the most recent write, or an error), availability (every request receives a non-error response, without a guarantee it's the most recent data), and partition tolerance (the system keeps operating despite dropped or delayed messages between nodes). The theorem is specifically about behavior during a partition - when there's no partition, a well-designed system can and should offer both consistency and availability, so CAP is not a claim about normal operation, only about what has to give when the network itself fails.

Because partitions are a physical reality on any network of more than one machine, partition tolerance in practice isn't really an optional design choice to trade away - it's a property distributed systems have to have, which reduces the real-world decision to CP versus AP: when a partition happens, does the system refuse requests it can't guarantee are consistent (CP, like a majority-quorum system such as etcd or Zookeeper), or does it keep answering with whatever data a node currently has, accepting that different nodes may disagree until the partition heals (AP, the classic example being a Dynamo-style store like Cassandra)?

A frequent misreading of CAP is treating it as a strict binary rather than a spectrum: most real systems are tunable per-operation rather than globally CP or globally AP. Cassandra, for instance, lets a client choose a consistency level (ONE, QUORUM, ALL) on each read or write, effectively picking a point along the C/A tradeoff for that specific request rather than the whole system committing to one side.

PACELC is often raised as CAP's necessary follow-up, because CAP alone says nothing about what happens when there is no partition: PACELC adds that even then, a system still has to trade latency against consistency (if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency), which is why a system like DynamoDB or Cassandra can be AP under partition and still offer a tunable consistency-versus-latency choice the rest of the time.

title: Rust ownership
content:
Rust's ownership system enforces, at compile time, that every value has exactly one owner and that the value is dropped (its memory freed) the moment that owner goes out of scope - no garbage collector runs to figure this out at runtime, and there's no way to double-free or use a value after it's gone, because the compiler statically tracks lifetimes and refuses to compile code where that could happen. Assigning a heap-allocated value to a new variable, or passing it into a function by value, moves ownership rather than copying it; the original binding is invalidated by the compiler, and any later use of it is a compile error rather than a runtime bug.

Borrowing lets code use a value without taking ownership of it, via references (&T for a shared, read-only borrow, &mut T for an exclusive, mutable one). The borrow checker enforces that at any point in the program, a value has either any number of shared borrows or exactly one mutable borrow, but never both at once - this single rule is what statically rules out data races on shared mutable state and iterator invalidation bugs, categories of bugs that in C++ or Java are only caught at runtime, if ever.

This is also why Rust doesn't need a garbage collector to be memory-safe: the compiler already knows, from the ownership graph alone, the exact point where a value's last owner goes out of scope, so it can insert the deallocation call there deterministically. The cost of that guarantee is that some perfectly safe patterns - two structs that both need to reference the same heap value, or a graph with cycles - don't fit the single-owner model cleanly, which is what Rc, Arc, and RefCell exist to handle by moving some of that checking from compile time to runtime in exchange for flexibility.

The borrow checker's rules are famously the biggest source of friction for people new to the language, because code that would run fine in most other languages - returning a reference to a local variable, holding a mutable and an immutable reference to the same data at once - simply won't compile in Rust, and the error has to be resolved by restructuring ownership rather than by finding a runtime bug later.
